JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concern (cross-sectional missing covariate data): While outcome and leadership variables cover all 82 counties in Guizhou Province (Table A2, PDF p. 25), listwise deletion due to missing data on Number of Villages (73/82) and Percentage Karst (70/82) reduces all regression models to N = 61 counties (25.6% sample loss; PDF pp. 15-16, 25-27). There is no longitudinal follow-up of completed water projects.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Cross-sectional observational OLS and prefecture-nested multilevel regressions adjust for observable economic, demographic, and geographic covariates (PDF pp. 13-19, 27), but lack any quasi-experimental causal identification strategy. Critically, true baseline county-level drinking water deficit/need is classified by the government and omitted, proxied only by the count of administrative villages (PDF p. 13). Unobserved political networks and historical project track records remain unmeasured confounders.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Statutory minority autonomous status is accurately operationalized at both the county level (11 autonomous counties) and prefecture level (3 autonomous prefectures) under PRC ethnic autonomy rules, correctly distinguishing statutory minority-reservation requirements for government governors from unreserved Communist Party secretary posts (PDF pp. 11-12, 18-19), and citing official National Rural Drinking Water Safety Project technical standards (PDF p. 9, fn. 1). However, sub-county de jure vs. de facto fiscal rules are not disaggregated.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Some concern: Census ethnic minority share, statutory autonomous status, and county leaders' biographical ethnicity (360 officials from CVs and news sources) are measured consistently, but outcomes rely on state-generated provincial Ministry of Water Resources (MWR) administrative project authorization records without independent verification of project completion or functionality, and projects approved without same-year completion are coded as zero budget/beneficiaries (PDF pp. 9-12, fn. 3).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate (adequate for administrative resource allocation; weak for actual safe water access): Dependent variables capture cumulative 2010-2013 MWR-authorized target beneficiaries and allocated funds from lightly processed internal records across 13,376 projects (PDF pp. 9-10), but explicitly do not measure physical infrastructure completion, maintenance, water quality compliance, or realized household drinking water access (PDF pp. 10, 20).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern: No preregistered protocol or pre-analysis plan exists. Several reporting anomalies appear in the published tables and text: Table 2 Model 1 misaligns the Geographic Controls rows (duplicating the Constant -99,780.18 into Slope and shifting Total Water Points/Karst, which is then interpreted substantively on PDF p. 18), PDF p. 16 misstates predicted RMB funding figures by conflating beneficiary counts with RMB units, and full-sample sensitivity regressions dropping incomplete covariates are asserted in prose (PDF p. 16) without tabulated estimates.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some concern: At the provincial frame level, the study covers the full administrative universe of all 82 counties in Guizhou Province and all 13,376 MWR-authorized projects from 2010 to 2013 (PDF pp. 8-9). However, Guizhou is purposively selected as a single poor, ethnically diverse province, and complete-case regression estimation excludes 21 of 82 counties (25.6%) with missing geographic/village-count covariates (PDF pp. 15-16, 25).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion criteria are clearly defined as the entire administrative universe of 82 counties in Guizhou Province and all 13,376 rural drinking water infrastructure projects authorized by the Guizhou provincial branch of the Ministry of Water Resources (MWR) between 2010 and 2013, alongside all 360 county Party secretaries and governors serving during 2010-2013.
domain_ratings.where_found: Research Design and Variables and Measurement, PDF pp. 8-12 (pp. 614-618); Appendix Table A2, PDF p. 25

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The institutional, geographic, and demographic context of rural Guizhou Province—including China's five-tier administrative structure, karst terrain, baseline rural water scarcity, ethnic composition (Han, Miao, Bouyi, Dong), the 11 autonomous counties and 3 autonomous prefectures, and summary statistics for all county variables—is described thoroughly.
domain_ratings.where_found: Research Design, PDF pp. 7-14 (pp. 613-620); Appendix Table A2, PDF p. 25

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: County ethnic minority share and diversity are drawn from the 2010 Chinese census, regional ethnic autonomy is coded from official PRC statutory administrative designations, and co-ethnic leadership is coded across alternative operationalizations (share Han leaders, governor vs. Party secretary ethnicity, titular minority status) from official CVs and news reports for 360 county leaders.
domain_ratings.where_found: Ethnic Concentration, Autonomy, and Co-ethnic Leaders subsections, PDF pp. 10-13 (pp. 616-619)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Official state census classifications of China's 55 recognized ethnic minority groups, formal statutory designation of minority autonomous counties/prefectures, and official provincial MWR project authorization logs provide standardized administrative criteria across all 82 counties.
domain_ratings.where_found: Variables and Measurement, Ethnic Concentration, and Autonomy subsections, PDF pp. 9-12 (pp. 615-618)

domain_ratings.justification: The author explicitly identifies economic (logged GDP per capita, local government fiscal expenditure), demographic (logged population, population density, urbanization share, outmigration, village count), and geographic (existing water points, karst coverage, average terrain slope) confounders, and transparently notes that direct baseline survey data on county drinking water deficits are classified and unavailable.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Multivariable OLS regressions, interaction models, variance inflation factor checks (VIF < 10), and prefecture-nested multilevel models (Table A5) are used to adjust for economic, demographic, and geographic confounders, using the number of administrative villages as a proxy for water infrastructure demand. Nevertheless, omitting classified baseline county water-access rates leaves substantial risk of residual confounding.
domain_ratings.where_found: Control Variables and Results sections, PDF pp. 13-19 (pp. 619-625); Appendix Tables A3-A5, PDF pp. 26-27

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes (cumulative 2010-2013 beneficiaries and funding) are compiled from lightly processed internal provincial MWR project records, which appropriately measure authorized resource allocation; however, approved projects not completed within the year are coded as zero budget/beneficiaries (fn. 3), state-generated administrative statistics are unaudited, and MWR provides no follow-up verification on whether projects were completed or actually delivered safe drinking water. Field visits also revealed redundant pipe-laying over existing water systems.
domain_ratings.where_found: Variables and Measurement, PDF pp. 9-10 (pp. 615-616, fn. 3); Control Variables, PDF p. 14 (p. 620); Conclusion, PDF p. 20 (p. 626)

domain_ratings.justification: Cross-sectional OLS with robust standard errors, multicollinearity checks (VIF < 10), and multilevel models nested in prefectures provide a reasonable descriptive-analytic baseline, but listwise deletion drops 21 of 82 counties (25.6%, leaving N = 61 with ~11-13 parameters on unlogged skewed outcome totals), full-sample sensitivity models without incomplete controls are untabulated, Table 2 Model 1 contains a row-shift/duplication error in the Geographic Controls block that distorts the text's discussion of slope vs. water points (PDF p. 18), and PDF p. 16 misreports predicted RMB funding units.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results, Tables 2-4, PDF pp. 14-19 (pp. 620-625); Appendix Tables A2-A5, PDF pp. 25-27

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Overall judgment: Some concern (JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies; Q1-Q6 Yes, Q7-Q8 Unclear). Pizzi (2020) conducts a cross-sectional county-level observational regression analysis of 13,376 Ministry of Water Resources (MWR) drinking water infrastructure projects authorized between 2010 and 2013 across Guizhou Province, aggregating cumulative project beneficiaries and funding to the county level. Key strengths include complete administrative frame coverage of Guizhou's 82 counties, clear operationalization of census ethnic minority share, statutory autonomous county/prefecture status, and county leaders' ethnicity (360 governors and CCP secretaries), and adjustment for economic, demographic, and geographic controls across OLS and prefecture-nested multilevel specifications. Methodological concerns center on four issues: (1) unmeasured baseline confounding, as official survey data on baseline county safe-water deficits are classified and proxied only by the count of administrative villages; (2) complete-case sample attrition of 25.6% (21 of 82 counties dropped in all regressions, leaving N = 61) due to missing village-count and karst data, with full-sample sensitivity checks asserted only narratively; (3) outcome measurement limited to authorized MWR allocations and target beneficiaries without verification of project completion, maintenance, or actual household safe water delivery; and (4) reporting inaccuracies in Table 2 Model 1 (misaligned geographic control rows duplicating the constant into Slope) and predicted funding figures on p. 622.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Quantitative analytical cross-sectional county-level observational regression study (aggregating 2010-2013 administrative project authorizations across counties in Guizhou Province, with brief illustrative field anecdotes)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research Design and Variables and Measurement, PDF pp. 7-14 (pp. 613-620); Results and Tables 2-4, PDF pp. 14-19 (pp. 620-625); Conclusion, PDF pp. 19-20 (pp. 625-626); Appendix Tables A1-A5, PDF pp. 25-27 (pp. 631-633).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The empirical analysis aggregates 2010-2013 Ministry of Water Resources project beneficiaries and funding into a single cumulative cross-section of Guizhou counties (N = 82 total; N = 61 in regressions) and estimates cross-sectional OLS and multilevel regressions without a longitudinal pre-post panel or quasi-experimental intervention comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I). Although the author briefly mentions field visits to over 50 villages and two informant remarks to illustrate mechanisms, the paper reports no qualitative research design, interview sampling, data collection protocol, or qualitative coding/analysis (ruling out MMAT). Accordingly, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching tool.
